newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO still waiting for its funds from Israel.
newsitem.headline: PLO still waiting for its funds from Israel.

text.p: The Palestinian Authority on Tuesday condemned Israel for violating peace deals as it awaited transfer of part of its funds frozen by the Jewish state after a July 30 double suicide bombing.

Israel, citing partial cooperation by the self-rule Authority in investigating the bombing that killed 16 people including the two attackers, said on Monday it would transfer 30 percent of the money to the Palestinians.
"The money has not been transferred yet," Palestinian Finance Minister Mohammad al-Nashashibi told Reuters.

"We believe all the money that is held to this moment should be transferred immediately. These Israeli measures harm all fields of the Palestinian economy. It's created a loss of $8 million to $9 million daily," he said.
An Israeli treasury spokesman told Reuters 42 million shekels ($12 million) would be transferred shortly.
"It could be today or tomorrow, but it is just technical," the spokesman said.

He said the funds would be transferred by the treasury to Palestinian Authority accounts held at Israeli banks. He would not name the banks. Nashashibi said the funds would ultimately move to local Palestinian banks.
The Treasury Ministry has said some 134 million shekels were frozen. Nashashibi said Israel had frozen a total of 180 million shekels.

After the Jerusalem bombing, Israel sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, disrupting trade and barring tens of thousands of Palestinians from jobs in Israel. It froze taxes and custom duties it owed the Authority under a 1994 economic protocol. The closure remains in effect.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has called the freeing of part of the funds a good start but not enough.

Israel says it will further ease sanctions in parallel with the Authority's fight against militants. The army said on Tuesday that it would grant 800 Palestinian traders entry. It also said it would allow cement and some other construction material into Gaza.

Hisham Abdel Razik, a Palestinian negotiator, told Israel Radio: "According to world opinion and also the United States, the Israeli government is the one that is not keeping the agreement and it is the one depending only on Israeli power."
The United States, which had said Israel's freezing of funds was counterproductive, has hailed the partial thaw.
Asked why the Palestinians were not waging a widescale crackdown on militants as Israel has demanded, Abdel Razik said it was still unclear who had carried out the bombing.
"The problem is that Israel understands that in a war against terror that the Palestinians have to put a significant portion of the Palestinian people in jail," Abdel Razik said.
"I think that what the prime minister wants is for the Palestinian people to fight one another," he added.

Palestinian security officials in a meeting with Israelis earlier this week handed over results of tests on explosives found in early July at what was thought to be a bomb laboratory of the anti-Israeli Hamas group, Israeli security sources said.
Israel Radio said tests on the explosives continued on Tuesday, witnessed by Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. officials.

The meeting was one in a series set up by U.S. envoy Dennis Ross last week. Ross was paving the way for a possible trip in September by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who has said she will come to the region if there is progress on security.
A leaflet in the name of Hamas claimed responsibility for the bombing but its authenticity has been questioned by Israeli and Palestinian officials. The attackers have yet to be identified.
The Authority in Gaza began this week blocking imports of non-essential Israeli products as part of a self-sufficiency drive spurred by the closure.
($1 = 3.52 shekels)
